passages.t: Pharaoh's daughter, and the high places
passages.happening:
“Later, Solomon formed an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter” (verse 1). He brings her to the City of David until his palace, the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem are finished.

The people are still sacrificing on the high places, ‘because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built’ (verse 2). “And Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The two notes that open the chapter are mild, but a reader who knows the law hears a warning in each.

A marriage to Pharaoh's daughter was a remarkable alliance. Egyptian kings of earlier times were known for refusing to send their daughters abroad as wives for foreign rulers. By Solomon's day Egypt was weaker and divided, ruled by the Twenty-first Dynasty from Tanis in the Nile delta, and such a match became more likely. The Bible does not name this Pharaoh. Some scholars suggest Siamun, but that is a proposal, not a certainty. Later the book says that Pharaoh captured Gezer and gave it to his daughter as a dowry (9:16).

High places were local hilltop shrines with altars, found throughout Canaan. Before the temple stood, Israelites worshiped the LORD at them, and the narrator explains rather than condemns: there was no house for the Name yet. But Deuteronomy had looked forward to one place of worship that God would choose, and later in Kings the high places become a mark of failure, even under good kings.

The small word except holds a reservation. Solomon's love for the LORD is real, and it is not yet whole.
passages.later: Deuteronomy had told Israel to seek ‘the place the LORD your God will choose from among all your tribes to establish as a dwelling for His Name’ (Deuteronomy 12:5). And it had warned that a king ‘must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray’ (Deuteronomy 17:17). Chapter 11 shows where Solomon's marriages led.
passages.hard:
Does the chapter approve of Solomon's worship at the high places?

Readers weigh it differently. Most interpreters see a gentle warning. The narrator explains the practice, since no temple yet existed, but he qualifies Solomon's devotion with the word except, and the high places will be a refrain of failure for the rest of the book. On this reading Solomon's heart for God is real, but it is not undivided, and the seed of compromise grows later.

Others see nothing negative here at all. They note that God meets Solomon at a high place, Gibeon, in the very next verses. Both readings agree that the chapter's main point is the gift of wisdom and its right use.
passages.asks: Solomon loved the LORD, except. Ask what your own except is: the place where your love for God makes room for something else. And ask which alliance you have made for safety or advantage might one day pull your heart.

passages.happening:
The king goes to Gibeon, ‘for it was the great high place’, and offers a thousand burnt offerings there (verse 4). That night the LORD appears to him in a dream: “Ask, and I will give it to you!” (verse 5).

Solomon remembers God's loving devotion to his father, ‘because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart’ (verse 6), and God's gift of a son on his throne. Then he speaks of himself: “But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in” (verse 7). He stands among a people too many to count. So he asks, “Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?” (verse 9).

“Now it pleased the Lord that Solomon had made this request” (verse 10). He had not asked for long life, or wealth, or the death of his enemies. God promises him ‘a wise and discerning heart’ (verse 12), and adds what he did not ask, riches and honor, and long life if he walks in God's ways as David did (verses 13-14).

Solomon wakes. He goes back to Jerusalem, stands before the ark of the covenant, offers sacrifices and holds a feast for all his servants (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Gibeon lay about six miles northwest of Jerusalem. Chronicles says that the tabernacle, the tent-sanctuary from Moses' day, stood there with its bronze altar at this time, which would explain why it was called the great high place. The ark itself was in Jerusalem, in the tent David had pitched for it, which is why Solomon goes back to stand before it.

Dreams were a known way for a god to speak to a king in that world. Royal inscriptions from Egypt and Mesopotamia tell of kings receiving divine messages in dreams, often at the start of a reign. What stands out here is the request. Solomon calls himself a little child who does not know how to go out or come in, a phrase for leading in battle and in daily life. He asks for no power and no revenge.

What he asks for is, in Hebrew, a hearing heart. The heart was the seat of thought and will, and a hearing heart listens to God and to the people it must judge. The same verb, shama, gives Israel's great confession its name, the Shema. And the word for discern means to tell things apart and see beneath appearances, which is exactly what the next case will need.

The king's first duty in that world was justice. Kings were the highest court of appeal, and ancient law collections such as Hammurabi's present the king as the one who establishes justice. Solomon asks for what the work demands.
passages.later:
Israel's great confession begins with the same verb: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Psalm 72, headed ‘Of Solomon’, prays, “Endow the king with Your justice, O God, and the son of the king with Your righteousness” (Psalm 72:1). Some read it as Solomon's own prayer at the start of his reign, and others as David's prayer for his son.

James tells the church, ‘Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him’ (James 1:5), and Solomon is the Bible's great example of someone who asked.
passages.asks: Solomon asked for what his people needed, not for what he wanted. Ask what you would ask for if God said to you, Ask. And ask whether you want a heart that listens, to God and to the people in your care, more than you want to be proved right.

passages.t: Two mothers and one living child
passages.happening:
Two prostitutes come and stand before the king (verse 16). One tells her story. The two of them live in the same house, and each gave birth, three days apart, with no one else there. ‘During the night this woman’s son died because she rolled over on him’ (verse 19), and, she says, the other woman took her living son from her side while she slept and laid the dead child in his place. In the morning she saw that the dead child was not her own (verses 20-21). The other woman says the living child is hers. They argue before the king.

Solomon repeats what each one says (verse 23). Then he asks for a sword and orders, “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other” (verse 25).

The mother of the living child ‘yearned with compassion for her son’ (verse 26) and begs the king to give the baby to the other woman rather than kill him. The other woman says, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” (verse 26). The king rules: “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother” (verse 27).

“When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The case has no witnesses, and each woman's story is the mirror of the other's. The king repeats both claims back word for word to show that the case is stuck. Then he cuts through it. The narrator does not tell the reader in advance what Solomon intends; the reader, like the court, learns the point only when the true mother cries out.

The word for her compassion, rachamim, is related to the word for womb. A mother's love gives her away. The same word is used of God's own compassion toward his people.

That two prostitutes could bring their case straight to the king says something important. Justice was meant to reach the lowest in the land. Here wisdom is shown not in clever sayings but in a just ruling for two women the city might have overlooked.

The last verse ties the chapter's two halves together. The gift Solomon asked for at Gibeon is seen in Jerusalem, and all Israel recognizes it as ‘the wisdom of God’ (verse 28).
passages.later: Psalm 72 prays for exactly this kind of king: “May he vindicate the afflicted among the people; may he save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor” (Psalm 72:4). And Proverbs says, ‘It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out’ (Proverbs 25:2).
passages.hard:
Would Solomon really have had the child killed? And what of the child who died?

The narrator does not say in advance what the king intends. The order works as a test: it shows which woman would rather lose her son than see him die. The text does not say what Solomon would have done if neither woman had spoken.

Behind the quarrel lies a death. A baby died in the night, and his mother's grief is never told; the story records the cause in one line and moves to what she did next. It is a story about the living child, and it does not linger over the one who was lost.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The true mother would give up her claim so that the child could live. Ask where love would have you give up being proved right. And ask whom you overlook who is owed justice as much as anyone.
